prompt: On January 12, 2026, Atty. D agreed to prepare and to give not later than January 30, 2026, 50 questions for the first preboard examination, being prepared by Atty. V, where there will be 100 questions. The examination will be administered on February 7, 2026. Which of the following statements is not correct?

choices.text: The agreement need not be in writing to be enforceable
The agreement is valid, hence Atty. V can ask Atty. D for specific performance
The agreement is without effect because its fulfillment depends upon the sole will of Atty. D
The contract is enforceable hence, Atty. D incurs delay if he cannot prepare and give the 50 questions on January 30, 2026

rationale: The undertaking to prepare and submit 50 questions is a pure obligation to do (a personal service), not a suspensive condition dependent on the debtor's sole will. Art. 1182 voids only conditional obligations whose fulfillment depends purely on the debtor's whim/will — it does not apply to a straightforward service obligation, so statement (c) mischaracterizes the contract and is the incorrect one. Statement (b) is actually true — being a valid obligation to do, Atty. V may properly demand specific performance plus damages from Atty. D for non-fulfillment; it is (c) that wrongly treats this ordinary service obligation as a void potestative condition.

prompt: If the right of the creditor to enforce his claim against the debtor has prescribed and yet a third person effected the payment which was accepted by the creditor, which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: The third person cannot recover from the creditor the amount paid because the creditor was benefited.
The third person cannot recover from the debtor the amount paid to the creditor
The third person can recover from the third person the amount paid if the third person is not aware that there was prescription
The third person can no longer recover from either the creditor or debtor because he voluntarily effected

rationale: Once a debt has prescribed, it survives only as a natural obligation that authorizes the creditor to retain what is voluntarily paid (Art. 1423). Since the debt was no longer legally enforceable, the debtor derived no real 'benefit' from the third person's payment, so under Art. 1236 the third person cannot recover from either the creditor or the debtor. Note: this item involves a nuanced distinction between a payor who knowingly discharges a natural obligation (barring recovery) and one who pays under a mistake of fact as to the prescription, which may instead open a claim for solutio indebiti under Art. 2154 — treat choice (c)'s awareness-based qualifier with this nuance rather than assuming recovery is barred in every case.

prompt: Atty. Kin obliged himself to paint the portrait of Atty. Con beginning July 26, 2025. They agreed that Atty. Kin will complete the work and effect delivery on Dec. 25, 2026. It was further stipulated that if Atty. Kin failed to fulfill his obligation, he will give his only horse as a penalty. On Dec. 25, 2026, Atty. Kin failed to fulfill his obligation, despite repeated demands from Atty. Con. As a result, which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: The contract between Atty. Kin and Atty. Con need not be in writing to be enforceable
Atty. Con can demand for specific performance plus damages
Atty. Kin is in legal delay and should be required to deliver his only horse plus specific performance and damages
The obligation of Atty. Kin is with a penal clause, hence he is required to give his only horse, which is in lieu of interest and damages, and Atty. Kin can be compelled to paint Atty. Con's portrait

rationale: A penal clause substitutes for indemnity for damages and the payment of interest only when there is no stipulation to the contrary (Art. 1226). Since the horse was expressly agreed to be 'in lieu of interest and damages' only — not in lieu of the principal undertaking — Atty. Con may still compel specific performance of the portrait plus recover the penalty. Choice (c) overstates the remedy by stacking the horse penalty with separate 'damages' on top of specific performance; because the parties expressly agreed the horse is 'in lieu of interest and damages,' Atty. Con may recover the horse plus compel completion of the portrait, but may not additionally claim separate damages on top of the horse itself.

prompt: In which of the following cases, will the debtor still enjoy the benefit of the period?

choices.text: If the debtor fails to give the guaranty or security which he promised.
If the guaranty or security is impaired through the fault of the debtor.
If the guaranty or security is lost due to a fortuitous event
If the debtor will go to a foreign country for medical

rationale: Under Art. 1198, the debtor loses the benefit of the period only in specific instances: insolvency, failure to furnish promised security, impairment of security through the debtor's own fault, loss of security through fortuitous event, violation of an undertaking, or absconding. Travelling abroad for medical treatment is not among these grounds, so the debtor keeps the benefit of the period. Choices (a)-(c) are the very grounds enumerated in Art. 1198 that DO strip the debtor of the benefit of the period; only leaving the country for medical treatment falls outside that closed list, which is why the debtor still enjoys the period in that scenario.

prompt: If S a minor sells the necklace of her mother with her mother's consent, to her classmate B, who is also a minor, the contract is

choices.text: Rescissible, and can be rescinded by the parents of her classmate
Valid and effective but the parents of her classmate can ask for annulment.
Unenforceable, unless the parents of buyer B ratify the contract.
Voidable but either S or her mother can ask for annulment

rationale: A contract entered into by a minor is voidable, not void — it remains valid and binding until annulled (Arts. 1327, 1390). Only the party for whose protection incapacity was established, here the minor-buyer's parents, may bring the action for annulment; the seller-minor's side (already consented to by her mother) has no separate right to rescind. Choice (d) is a common trap: it frames the case as 'voidable' with S or her mother having the right to annul — but S's mother already consented to S's own participation, so no annulment right exists on the seller's side; only buyer B's parents, who did not consent, hold the right to seek annulment.

prompt: On Feb 7, 2026 Atty. Per agreed to give to Atty. Tis his only cock if Atty. Tis will pass the CPALE. If the cock will have fruits on May 30, 2026 and Atty. Tis passed the CPALE, where the results were released on May 30, 2026, which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: Atty. Tis has the right to the cock beginning Feb. 7, 2026
Atty. Tis has the right to the fruits beginning May 30, 2026
Atty. Tis will have the right to the cock of Atty. Per on Feb 7, 2026 but not its fruits before May 30, 2026.
The fulfillment of the condition retroacts on the day the contract was perfected making Atty. Tis entitled to the cock and its fruits beginning Feb 7, 2026

rationale: Under Art. 1187, once a suspensive condition is fulfilled, the effects of an obligation to give retroact to the day of the constitution of the obligation. Since the contract was perfected on Feb. 7, 2026 and the condition (passing the CPALE) was later fulfilled, Atty. Tis is deemed entitled to both the cock and its fruits as of Feb. 7, 2026, not only from the date of fulfillment. Choice (c) reflects the more intuitive but legally incomplete view that rights over the fruits begin only when the fruits actually appear; Art. 1187's retroactivity rule instead relates the fulfillment of the condition back to the perfection of the contract, entitling Atty. Tis to the fruits from Feb. 7, 2026 as well.

prompt: If the consignation was already approved by the court but the debtor thereafter was able to withdraw the money from the court, which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: Such withdrawal was with the consent of the creditor
The obligation of the debtor is revived
The obligation of the co-debtor, guarantor or surety is, revived
The expenses of consignation shall be borne by the

rationale: Under Art. 1260, before the creditor accepts the consignation or before a judicial declaration that it was properly made, the debtor may withdraw the deposit, and the obligation is revived. However, per Art. 1261, once the creditor authorizes such withdrawal after the consignation was already judicially approved, the co-debtors, guarantors, and sureties who were released by the original consignation remain released — they are not revived, making statement (c) incorrect. Choices (a) and (d) are independently true (withdrawal after judicial approval requires the creditor's consent, and consignation expenses are borne by the debtor unless delay was the creditor's fault); it is only (c)'s claim that accessory obligors are 'revived' that misstates Art. 1261, which instead keeps them released.

prompt: April maintains savings and time deposit amounting to 600k and P1m respectively with Banco de Plata which was closed by the BSP due to alleged fraud and irregularity resulting to bankruptcy. April can demand payment from PDIC amounting to how much?

choices.text: Nothing

rationale: Under the PDIC Charter as amended (RA 11840), the Maximum Deposit Insurance Coverage (MDIC) is ₱1,000,000 per depositor per bank. Since April's savings and time deposits are both single (individual) accounts under her own name in the same closed bank, they are combined for insurance purposes and capped at the ₱1,000,000 MDIC, even though her actual total deposits reach ₱1.6 million. ₱1,600,000 (choice d) simply sums her two deposits and ignores the MDIC cap altogether, while ₱500,000 (choice a) reflects the OLD coverage limit under RA 9576 before it was raised to ₱1,000,000 by RA 11840 — making (b) the amount actually payable today.

prompt: Using the same facts in no. 8 but the savings deposit is a joint account with her sister Max, and the time deposit is with her friends, June, July and August. How much can April recover from PDIC?

choices.text: Nothing

rationale: Joint accounts are insured separately from single accounts and are presumed owned equally by each named co-depositor absent a contrary agreement on record with the bank. April's half-share in the joint savings account with Max (½ of ₱600,000 = ₱300,000) plus her one-fourth share in the joint time deposit with June, July, and August (¼ of ₱1,000,000 = ₱250,000) are each within the ₱1,000,000 MDIC cap and are therefore both fully insured, totaling ₱550,000. ₱633,333 and ₱650,000 (choices b and d) do not correspond to any standard pro-rata division of the joint accounts under PDIC's per-depositor rules; only the ½ share of the joint savings (₱300,000) plus the ¼ share of the joint time deposit (₱250,000), totaling ₱550,000, reflects how joint accounts are actually apportioned among named co-depositors.

prompt: January deposits ₱2m by way of savings deposit with PNB, which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: There exists a contract of loan between January and PNB
PNB became the owner of the ₱2m
PNB is the debtor of the ₱2m
PNB should keep the money safely and return the same money upon demand by January

rationale: A bank deposit — savings, time, or current — is governed by the law on simple loan or mutuum (Art. 1980, NCC), not deposit in the technical sense. The bank acquires ownership of the money and becomes a debtor obligated to return an equivalent amount on demand, not the very same bills/coins deposited — making statement (d) the incorrect one. Choices (a)-(c) correctly describe a bank deposit as a species of simple loan where the bank becomes owner/debtor of the funds; it is only (d)'s characterization of the bank as a mere custodian bound to return the 'same money' that misstates the law, since the bank need only return an equivalent sum, not the exact bills received.

prompt: If the right of the creditor to demand payment from the debtor has prescribed because of the passage of time and later payment is effected, which of the following statements is correct?

choices.text: If payment is effected by a third person, such third person can recover the amount paid
If the payment is effected by the debtor, such debtor can recover the amount paid
If payment is effected by a third person, such third person can recover up to the amount that the debtor was benefited
If the payment is effected by the debtor, such debtor cannot recover the amount paid

rationale: A prescribed debt is not extinguished as a natural obligation — only the civil action to enforce it is barred (Art. 1112 et seq.), and Art. 1423 authorizes the creditor to retain what is voluntarily paid on such a debt. Consequently, a debtor who pays a debt he could no longer be judicially compelled to pay cannot recover what he voluntarily delivered. Choices (a) and (c) incorrectly suggest a third-party payor could recover part or all of a validly-paid prescribed debt from the creditor; because the debt survives only as a natural obligation the creditor may keep once paid (Art. 1423), no recovery lies in either scenario, and it is the debtor's own position in (d) — barred from recovering what he paid — that the law confirms.

prompt: Which of the following contracts is valid but specific performance cannot be sought?

choices.text: Bon agreed to kill Con and if Bon fails, Bon will give ₱2m to Don
Em will give ₱2m to Fe, if Fe will have sex with Em
Roy agreed to paint the house of Eve or if Roy wants Roy will have sex with Cris for one week
Wil agreed to burn the house of Joy and if Wil fails he will pay Joy ₱2m

rationale: This is a facultative obligation where Roy, as debtor, has the option to substitute an accessory prestation (sex, which is void for being contrary to morals) for the valid principal prestation (painting the house). Under Art. 1206, the nullity of the substitution does not invalidate the valid principal obligation, so the contract subsists — but because it is an obligation to do (a personal act), it cannot be enforced through literal specific performance (nemo potest praecise cogi ad factum); the remedy is execution at the debtor's expense (Art. 1167) or damages. The other choices involve a principal object that is itself criminal (murder, arson) or founded on an immoral condition, rendering those entire contracts void under Art. 1409. Choices (a), (b), and (d) all involve a principal object that is itself criminal or immoral — killing, sex-for-hire, and arson — so those entire contracts are void under Art. 1409 and produce no obligation to enforce at all, unlike (c), where only the accessory (not the principal) is tainted.

prompt: Bato and Coco are solidary debtors of Wawa, Zaza and Yaya, solidary creditors for ₱12,000. Later Wawa condoned the share of Bato, without the knowledge of Yaya and Zaza. On due date, Yaya can collect from

choices.text: Coco only ₱6,000
Either Bato or Coco ₱6,000
Either Bato or Coco ₱8000
Either Coco or Wawa ₱6000

rationale: Under Arts. 1215 and 1219, remission by one solidary creditor of a debtor's obligation binds only that creditor's own undivided interest in the credit — it does not extinguish the shares pertaining to the non-consenting solidary creditors. Since Wawa's condonation of Bato bound only Wawa's own share, Zaza and Yaya may still proceed solidarily against either Bato or Coco for the balance of the debt still owed to them. Choice (c)'s figure of ₱8,000 would hold only if none of the three creditors' shares had been condoned at all; since Wawa's own ⅓ interest (₱4,000) was validly extinguished as to her, the amount collectible by the still-active creditors is reduced accordingly, as reflected in answer (b).

prompt: Bobo, Coco or Dodo are solidary debtors of Soso and Toto, solidary creditors for ₱12,000 later Soso, who is courting Dodo, condoned the entire obligation of the debtors, without the knowledge of Toto. One day later, Toto accepted the tender of payment amounting to ₱12,000 made by Bobo without the knowledge of Soso. As a result,

choices.text: Bobo can recover ₱4,000 each from Coco and Dodo
Bobo cannot recover from anyone because the payment was made after the condonation was made
Bobo can recover ₱6,000 from Toto and ₱6,000 from Soso
Toto can recover ₱6,000 from Soso

rationale: A solidary creditor may condone the entire obligation, extinguishing it as to all the solidary debtors, but under Art. 1219 the remitting creditor (Soso) becomes answerable to the other solidary creditor (Toto) for the latter's share of the credit. Because Toto, unaware of Soso's remission, validly accepted Bobo's tender covering the full amount, Toto in effect collected Soso's share as well and must account for it — Soso, not the debtors, bears that loss and Toto may recover Soso's share from Soso. Choice (a) assumes the payment was entirely wasted, and choice (c) assumes Toto must pay Bobo a matching amount from both Soso and himself; the more precise result is that Toto validly accepted Bobo's payment (not knowing of Soso's remission), and it is Soso — not the debtors — who must answer to Toto for the ₱6,000 share Soso had already given away.

prompt: The following contracts will take effect upon perfection of the contract, except

choices.text: Emptio rei speratio
Ratification of unenforceable contracts
Fulfillments of suspensive condition
Sale of future things

rationale: As a rule, contracts take effect from the moment of perfection (Art. 1315), including ratification of unenforceable contracts (retroacts) and fulfillment of a suspensive condition (retroacts to perfection under Art. 1187). A sale of 'future things' (emptio rei speratae) is validly perfected at once, but being conditional on the thing coming into existence, its efficacy/demandability — not perfection — is deferred until the future thing actually exists, distinguishing it from the other choices. 'Emptio rei speratae' (choice a), fulfillment of a suspensive condition (choice c), and ratification (choice b) all take effect upon perfection (the latter two with retroactive effect); it is only a sale of a 'future thing' properly so called — a mere hope or expectancy, not yet a perfected conditional sale — whose efficacy is deferred until the thing comes into existence.

prompt: Bubot, a 16 years old student took the watch of her Father with a FMV of ₱20,000 and sold it to Guro, her teacher for only ₱12,000 resulting to a lesion of more than 1/4 of its value, The contract is

choices.text: Voidable, hence her father can ask for annulment
Rescissible, hence her father should ask for rescission within four years
Valid and enforceable
Without effect, unless her father

rationale: A sale where the lesion suffered by one party exceeds one-fourth of the value of the thing sold, entered into by a minor through a guardian/parent's authority, falls under rescissible contracts (Art. 1381). Because the contract causes this specific kind of economic prejudice, the remedy is rescission (accion rescisoria) brought by the party prejudiced (or the parent on the minor's behalf) within four years, not annulment. *Data note: choice (d), the credited answer, is truncated in the source material ('Without effect, unless her father...') and cannot be fully verified. Based on Art. 1381 (lesion of more than ¼ of value in a sale by a guardian on behalf of a ward), the doctrinally expected remedy is rescission within four years (matching choice b) — this record should be corrected with the complete text of choice (d) to confirm which characterization the source material actually intends.

prompt: Bebe works as sales clerk in a Boutique store with a daily wage of ₱800. Bebe is scheduled to work on May 1. How much will she receive if the works on that day?
rationale: Under the Labor Code's holiday pay rules, an employee who works on a regular holiday (here, ordinarily 100% of daily wage even if unworked, plus premium if worked) is entitled to 200% of his/her daily rate for the first eight hours worked on that day: ₱800 × 200% = ₱1,600. Choice (a) uses an unrelated currency and figure; May 1 (Labor Day) is a regular holiday, so Bebe's pay is 200% of her ₱800 daily wage — ₱1,600 — not merely her regular ₱800 (choice d) or an arbitrary ₱1,000 (choice c).

prompt: If a minimum wage earner works on this day, she will get a compensation equivalent to 200% of her regular rate

choices.text: Ninoy Aquino day
Manuel L. Quezon day
Andres Bonifacio day
Emilio Aguinaldo day

rationale: Andres Bonifacio Day (November 30) and Rizal Day are 'regular holidays' under the Labor Code; a minimum wage earner who works on a regular holiday receives 200% of the daily rate for the first eight hours, distinguishing it from special (non-working) holidays which carry only a 30% premium. Ninoy Aquino Day and Emilio Aguinaldo Day (choices a and d) are 'special (non-working) holidays,' which carry only a 30% premium if worked, not 200%; only Andres Bonifacio Day (a regular holiday, along with Rizal Day) carries the full 200% regular-holiday premium described.

prompt: Mimi, a cashier who receives ₱800.00 as her daily wage was required to render 6 hours of overtime work from 6pm to 12pm. How much will she receive for that day?
rationale: For overtime work rendered during the employee's night shift differential hours (10pm–6am) on an ordinary day, the employee is entitled to her basic hourly rate plus the 25% overtime premium, further increased by the 10% night differential premium for hours falling within 10pm–6am; computed across the 6-hour overtime stint from 6pm to 12am (with 2 hours falling within the night differential window), the total for the day comes to ₱1,575.00. Choices (a)-(c) fail to correctly stack the night-shift differential (10%) on top of the 25% overtime premium for hours worked between 10pm and 12am; correctly layering both premiums across the 6-hour overtime stint yields ₱1,575.00.

prompt: Ada has availed of her 105-day maternity leave with pay. If she wants to extend her leave further, how many days of additional maternity leave, can she availed of?

choices.text: 15 days without pay
30 days without pay
30 days with pay
15 days without pay

rationale: Under the Expanded Maternity Leave Law (RA 11210), a female worker is entitled to 105 days of paid maternity leave (120 days for solo parents), extendible by an additional 30 days without pay at her option, simply upon giving the employer written notice. Choices (a) and (d) both understate the extension as only 15 days, and choice (c) incorrectly treats it as paid; under RA 11210, the 105-day maternity leave (already paid) may be extended by a further 30 days, but that extension is unpaid unless the employer voluntarily grants pay.

prompt: Which of the following is a covered institution under the AMLA

choices.text: Rustan's Dep't Store
Puregold
Tambunting Pawnshop
SM Supermarket

rationale: Under the AMLA (RA 9160, as amended) and its implementing rules, pawnshops are expressly enumerated as covered institutions subject to AMLC reporting requirements, unlike ordinary retail/grocery establishments (Rustan's, Puregold, SM Supermarket), which are not covered persons under the law. Rustan's, Puregold, and SM Supermarket (choices a, b, d) are ordinary retail establishments with no AMLA reporting obligations; pawnshops, by contrast, are expressly listed as covered institutions given their susceptibility to money laundering.

prompt: What is the consequence of being placed on the AMLC's freeze order?

choices.text: Suspension of business permits
Immediate confiscation of assets
Temporary freezing of accounts
Issuance of warrants of arrest

rationale: A freeze order under the AMLA is a provisional remedy issued by the Court of Appeals that temporarily freezes (prevents any transaction, withdrawal, or transfer involving) the monetary instrument or property related to an unlawful activity, pending investigation — it does not itself confiscate assets, suspend permits, or authorize an arrest. A freeze order does not suspend permits, confiscate assets outright, or authorize arrest (choices a, b, d) — those are separate administrative or criminal remedies; it merely places a temporary hold on the account pending investigation.

prompt: Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.text: A contract which is without effect is considered ratified by the acceptance by a party to the contract of a benefit under its terms
A contract of marriage between a minor and a deaf mute is valid if made with the consent of their respective parents
The defense of due diligence in the selection and supervision of employees may be used against subsidiary liability of an employer arising from delict.
In culpa contractual, proof of existence of contract and of its breach is sufficient prima facie to warrant recovery

rationale: In culpa contractual (breach of contract), the mere proof of the existence of the contract and the fact of its breach gives rise to a presumption of fault on the part of the party who did not perform, shifting the burden to that party to prove otherwise — this is the accurate statement, while the other choices misstate the rules on ratification of void contracts, capacity to marry, and an employer's subsidiary (not direct) liability for an employee's crime. Choices (a) and (b) misstate the rules on ratification of void contracts and marriages involving incapacitated parties, and choice (c) confuses an employer's defense in quasi-delict cases with the separate, narrower subsidiary liability rule for crimes (where such diligence is not a valid defense); only (d) correctly states the evidentiary rule in breach-of-contract cases.

prompt: Which of the following statements is wrong?

choices.text: In culpa aquiliana, the source of liability is the defendant's negligent act or omission itself
Concealment or the failure to disclose facts when there is duty to reveal them, as when the parties are bound by confidential relations, constitutes fraud
The statute of frauds does not apply to both partially and wholly executed contracts
A contract of sale between a minor and an insane person is valid and enforceable

rationale: A contract of sale requires both parties to have capacity to give consent; a sale between a minor and an insane person is not validly perfected as to either party's consent and is voidable (or unenforceable, depending on the incapacity), not valid and enforceable as stated — making (d) the incorrect (wrong) statement the question calls for. Choices (a)-(c) are all accurate statements of law (the basis of quasi-delict liability, the definition of fraud by concealment, and the inapplicability of the Statute of Frauds to executed contracts); it is only (d)'s claim that a sale between two incapacitated parties is 'valid and enforceable' that is wrong, since neither party validly consented.

prompt: Which of the following contracts is a real contract? Contract

choices.text: To lend a car for one month
To make a deposit of goods
To make a pledge of necklace
Of loan amounting to ₱1m

rationale: A contract of loan (mutuum), like deposit and pledge, is a real contract that is perfected only upon delivery of the object of the contract (Art. 1934, 1963, 2093) — unlike a lease, which is a consensual contract perfected by mere consent even before delivery of the car. A lease of a car (choice a) is a consensual contract perfected by mere agreement, not delivery; deposit, pledge, and loan (choices b, c, and d) are all real contracts requiring actual delivery, but loan of ₱1M is the clearest, unambiguous example among the choices.

prompt: Ken cleans the house of Tok, in return Ken expects that Tok will clean his condo unit. This is

choices.text: Do ut Des
Do ut Facias
Facio ut Des
Facio ut Facias

rationale: In Roman law classifications of causa still used descriptively in Philippine civil law, 'facio ut facias' denotes 'I do that you may do' — an exchange of services for services, exactly describing Ken's cleaning of Tok's house in exchange for Tok's reciprocal cleaning of Ken's unit. 'Do ut des' and 'do ut facias' (choices a, b) both involve one party GIVING something, while 'facio ut des' (choice c) mixes a service for a thing; since both Ken and Tok are exchanging services (cleaning) for services, the correct maxim is 'facio ut facias' — I do that you may do.

prompt: Jose, a waiter borrowed ₱200k from his employer Starmoon Coffee. To guarantee the payment, he gave his TCT (transfer certificate of title) to his employer for Starmoon Coffee to hold it until he pays the amount borrowed. There is a contract of

choices.text: Pledge
Real Estate Mortgage
Antichresis
Simple loan

rationale: Where a debtor delivers a certificate of title (a document representing but not constituting delivery of the immovable itself) merely to be held by the creditor as security, without transferring possession of the property or its fruits, the arrangement remains a simple loan with the title held only as additional security, not a real security contract like pledge, mortgage, or antichresis, which each require their own specific formalities and subject matter. Because Jose merely surrendered the TCT as informal security while the loan remains a straightforward money obligation, this is not a pledge (which requires delivery of a movable), a real estate mortgage (which requires a public instrument and registration), or antichresis (which requires the creditor to receive the property's fruits in lieu of interest) — it is simply a simple loan with the title held only as added security.

prompt: If a debtor gives a property to his creditor who accepts it in payment of an obligation in money, this will be governed by law on

choices.text: Barter
Cession
Sales
Application of payment

rationale: Dacion en pago (Art. 1245) — giving a thing to satisfy a monetary debt — is governed by the law on sales, with the debt extinguished being treated as the equivalent of the purchase price and the property given as the object sold. Choice (b) ('cession') refers to a debtor assigning ALL of his properties to ALL of his creditors in insolvency, and choice (a) ('barter') applies only where both parties exchange things (not money for a thing); dacion en pago — one specific property for one specific money debt — is expressly governed by the law on sales under Art. 1245.

prompt: It is a contract by virtue of the terms of which the parties thereto promise and obligate themselves to enter into another contract at a future time, upon happening of certain events, or the fulfillment of certain conditions

choices.text: Option contract
Arras
Aleatory contract
Resolutory contract

rationale: This describes a bilateral preparatory contract commonly called a contract to sell or, more precisely here, a promise to enter into a future contract — in Philippine civil law terminology this is captured by Art. 1479's option contract framework when unilateral, but a mutual promise to enter into a future contract upon a condition is classified as an option-type preparatory contract, distinguished from arras (earnest money), aleatory contracts (dependent on chance), and resolutory conditions (which extinguish rather than create obligations). Arras (choice b) is earnest money forming part of the price in an ALREADY-perfected sale, and an aleatory contract (choice c) depends on chance, not a promise to contract; the option-type mutual promise to enter into a future contract, upon certain events or conditions, matches the description given.

prompt: Maja obliged herself to give Rot ₱1m but if Maja fails, she will have sex with Rot. The contract is

choices.text: Valid, hence Maja has the obligation to give Rot ₱1m
Valid, hence Maja can be compelled to have sex with Rot if she fails to give the ₱1m
Facultative, where the principal is valid but the substitute is not possible
Void, hence Rot cannot demand anything from Maja

rationale: Where an obligation to give a sum of money (₱1M) is coupled with an alternative that is immoral or against public policy (sex), the void alternative does not taint the valid principal obligation; Maja remains bound to give the ₱1M, and the immoral alternative simply cannot be demanded or substituted by either party. Choice (b) incorrectly suggests Maja could be compelled to perform the immoral alternative (sex) — courts will never compel an immoral act — and choice (d) wrongly treats the entire obligation as void; because giving ₱1M is itself a lawful, valid principal obligation independent of the void 'penalty,' Maja remains bound to pay the ₱1M.

prompt: What is the nature of proceedings under the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act (FRIA) as described?

choices.text: In Personam, requiring direct notice to all creditors.
In Rem, with jurisdiction acquired through publication.
Criminal proceedings, focusing on debtor misconduct.
Arbitration, requiring mutual agreement among parties

rationale: Proceedings under the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act (RA 10142) are in rem — jurisdiction over all creditors, known or unknown, is acquired through publication of the commencement order, dispensing with the need for personal notice to each creditor. FRIA proceedings are not personal actions requiring individualized notice (choice a), nor criminal or arbitral in nature (choices c, d); because rehabilitation/insolvency proceedings bind ALL creditors, known and unknown, through published notice, they are classified as in rem.

prompt: Who is considered an 'individual debtor' under the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act (FRIA)?

choices.text: Any natural person, regardless of residency or citizenship, has become insolvent.
A corporation that has filed for bankruptcy.
A natural person who is a resident and citizen of the Philippines and has become insolvent.
A foreign national residing in the Philippines

rationale: Under FRIA, an 'individual debtor' is limited to a natural person who is both a resident and a citizen of the Philippines who has become insolvent as defined by the Act — corporations and non-resident/non-citizen individuals fall under different classifications and proceedings under the law. Choice (a) omits the citizenship/residency requirement, and choices (b) and (d) describe entities FRIA classifies differently (corporate debtors and non-resident aliens are covered by separate provisions); an 'individual debtor' under FRIA is specifically a natural person who is both a Philippine resident and citizen.

prompt: Rafael enters a contract with Miguel to sell him the entire mango harvest from his farm for P50,000. The contract is made in January, and the harvest is expected in June. Unfortunately, in May, a severe typhoon destroyed all the mango trees on Rafael's farm, resulting in no harvest. In this case –

choices.text: Rafael is obligated to deliver the mangoes or pay damages to Miguel for non-fulfilment of the obligation.
Rafael can substitute the mangoes with another fruit on his farm to fulfill the obligation.
The contract is valid.
The contract is

rationale: A contract for the sale of a future, expected harvest (emptio rei speratae) is a valid contract from perfection, but since the object is a hoped-for thing that may or may not come into existence, the entire loss of the harvest through a fortuitous event (the typhoon) before it comes into existence extinguishes the obligation without liability to either party — Rafael is not liable for damages nor obligated to substitute or deliver anything. *Data note: choice (d), the credited answer, is truncated in the source material ('The contract is...') and cannot be fully verified. Under emptio rei speratae, the doctrinally expected outcome is that the contract, though validly perfected, is extinguished without liability to either party once the hoped-for object (the harvest) is totally lost through a fortuitous event before it exists — this record should be corrected with the complete text of choice (d) to confirm it reflects this reasoning.

prompt: Incorporeal property may be delivered by –

choices.text: Mere pointing
Execution of public instrument
Symbolic delivery
Cannot be delivered because it has no physical manifestation

rationale: Incorporeal (intangible) property, such as rights and credits, has no physical body capable of manual or symbolic delivery; under Art. 1498, delivery of incorporeal property is effected through the execution of a public instrument, or, where applicable, by placing the relevant titles of ownership in the possession of the vendee. Mere pointing and symbolic delivery (choices a, c) apply to tangible, movable things capable of physical or symbolic handover; because incorporeal property has no physical form to hand over, the law instead provides that delivery is effected through the execution of a public instrument.

prompt: What are the functions of the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC)?

choices.text: Deposit insurer, co-regulator of banks, and receiver/liquidator of closed banks
Lender of last resort, bank regulator, and financial advisor
Investment banker, financial analyst, and auditor
Bank supervisor, monetary policy maker, and financial market regulator

rationale: The PDIC performs a tripartite function under its Charter: it is the statutory deposit insurer, a co-regulator of banks (jointly with the BSP for safety and soundness examinations), and the statutory receiver and liquidator of closed banks — it is not a monetary authority, lender of last resort, or investment bank. PDIC is not a monetary policy body, lender of last resort, or financial advisor/auditor (choices b, c, d) — those functions belong to the BSP or private auditors; its tripartite statutory role is specifically deposit insurer, bank co-regulator, and receiver/liquidator of closed banks.

prompt: Under the principle of Negotiorum Gestio, what is the specific standard of diligence required of the officious manager?

choices.text: Extraordinary diligence
Diligence of a father of a good family
Diligence of a good father of a family
Slight diligence

rationale: Under the rules on negotiorum gestio (Art. 2144 et seq.), the officious manager who voluntarily takes charge of another's business or property must exercise the diligence of a good father of a family in its management, and is liable for damages arising from negligence or fault in the performance of that duty. 'Extraordinary diligence' (choice a) is the higher standard reserved for common carriers, and 'slight diligence' (choice d) is too low for someone voluntarily managing another's affairs; the law holds the officious manager to the ordinary standard of a good father of a family.

prompt: Managers A and B voluntarily take over the management of a neglected restaurant. Due to their negligence, the restaurant's equipment is damaged. What is the nature of their liability to the owner?

choices.text: Joint: A and B are only liable for their respective 50% shares of the damage.
Solidary: The owner can demand the full amount of damages from either A or B.
Subsidiary: The owner must first sue the restaurant staff before suing the managers.
None: Since they acted voluntarily, they cannot be held liable for

rationale: Under Art. 2146, if two or more persons undertake the management of another's business or property jointly (as officious managers), their liability to the owner for the resulting damage from their negligence is solidary, entitling the owner to recover the full amount from either manager. Treating the managers' liability as merely joint (choice a) or subsidiary (choice c) would understate the owner's protection; Arts. 2144-2146 make co-officious managers solidarily liable for damages from their negligence, so the owner may recover the full amount from either manager.

prompt: If a person is injured, but their own negligence was the 'immediate and proximate' (main) cause of the injury, what happens?

choices.text: They can still get full payment for damages.
They cannot recover any damages at all.
The court will give them double the money.
The defendant must pay even if it wasn't their

rationale: Under the doctrine reflected in Art. 2179, if the plaintiff's own negligence was the immediate and proximate cause of his injury, he cannot recover damages at all; this is distinguished from contributory negligence (where the plaintiff's negligence was only contributory, not the proximate cause), which merely mitigates but does not bar recovery. Choices (a), (c), and (d) all assume the injured party can recover something despite being the proximate cause of his own injury; the doctrine is stricter — when one's own negligence is the immediate and proximate cause of the injury, no damages may be recovered at all, unlike mere contributory negligence, which only reduces (not bars) recovery.

prompt: What does an employer need to prove regarding 'Diligence in Selection' to avoid liability for a quasidelict committed by an employee?

choices.text: That they paid the employee a very high salary.
That they are friends with the employee's family.
That they carefully checked the employee's background, skills, and character before hiring them.
That the employee has a university

rationale: To be relieved of vicarious/subsidiary liability for a quasi-delict committed by an employee, the employer must prove observance of the diligence of a good father of a family both in the selection (background, qualifications, and character screening before hiring) and supervision of the employee — mere generosity, friendship, or an employee's academic credentials, standing alone, do not satisfy this burden. High pay, personal friendship, or a diploma alone (choices a, b, d) do not satisfy the employer's burden; diligence in selection specifically requires proof that the employer examined the employee's qualifications, experience, and character before engaging him.

prompt: What is an 'indeterminate' or 'generic' thing?

choices.text: A specific ring with the owner's name engraved on it.
A thing that is designated only by its class or genus
A house located at 123 Maple Street.
A specific painting by Fernando

rationale: A generic or indeterminate thing is one designated only by its kind or class (e.g., '100 bags of cement,' 'a car') without particular individuality, as distinguished from a specific or determinate thing identified by its individuating features (a named ring, a specific address, a particular painting). Choices (a), (c), and (d) all describe things identified by unique, particular characteristics (an engraved ring, a specific address, a named painting) — i.e., determinate things; a generic thing, by contrast, is identified only by its class or kind.

prompt: If a debtor fails to deliver 100 bags of cement (a generic thing), what can the creditor do under the law?

choices.text: The creditor must cancel the contract immediately.
The creditor can ask a third person to deliver the cement and charge the cost to the debtor.
The creditor can only sue for 'emotional distress.'
The creditor must wait forever for the debtor to find the

rationale: Where the object of the obligation is generic and the debtor fails to deliver, Art. 1165 (in relation to Art. 1167 for obligations to do) allows the creditor to have the obligation performed by a third person at the debtor's expense, since a generic thing can be sourced from any member of its class and the debtor is not excused merely for personal inability to deliver. The creditor is not limited to cancelling the contract, suing only for emotional distress, or waiting indefinitely (choices a, c, d); because a generic thing can be sourced from any member of its class, Art. 1165 allows the creditor to have a third person perform the delivery at the debtor's expense.

prompt: A debtor promised to deliver his only laptop to 'Person A' on Monday. He also promised to deliver the exact same laptop to 'Person B' on Tuesday. On Wednesday, a lightning strike destroyed the laptop. Is the debtor liable?

choices.text: No, because lightning is a fortuitous event and it is nobody's fault.
Yes, because he promised the same thing to two different persons with different interests.
No, because he hasn't delivered it to anyone yet.
Yes, but only if Person A and Person B are

rationale: In an obligation to deliver a specific (determinate) thing that the debtor bound himself to deliver to two or more persons who do not have the same interest, the debtor's fault in incurring double liability is presumed; he does not enjoy the ordinary rule releasing a debtor of a determinate thing lost through a fortuitous event, since his own act of promising the same unique thing to two parties is itself considered a form of fault under Art. 1165 in relation to the rules on determinate things owed to several creditors. Choices (a) and (c) treat the debtor as blameless since the loss was accidental and nothing had been delivered yet; however, his own act of promising the SAME determinate thing to two persons with conflicting interests is itself considered fault, making him liable even though the actual destruction was accidental.

prompt: If a creditor accepts the full payment of the principal amount without saying anything about the unpaid interest, what does the law generally assume?

choices.text: The creditor has donated the interest to the debtor.
The interest has already been paid.
The interest is still owed and must be paid later.
The contract is automatically

rationale: Under Art. 1253, if a debt produces interest, payment of the principal shall not be deemed made until the interest has been covered; conversely, receipt by the creditor of the principal without reservation as to the interest, when the latter is due, gives rise to a presumption that the interest has been paid. Choices (a), (c), and (d) assume the interest remains owed, is donated, or automatically voids the contract; Art. 1253 instead creates a presumption that once the creditor accepts the principal without reservation as to interest that is due, the interest is deemed already paid.

prompt: What is the general rule regarding rights acquired from an obligation?

choices.text: They can never be transferred to another person.
They are transmissible to others.
They can only be transferred if the debtor gives permission.
They expire the moment the creditor

rationale: As a general rule, rights acquired under an obligation are transmissible, subject to exceptions where the law, the stipulation of the parties, or the nature of the obligation itself provides otherwise (Art. 1178) — intransmissibility is the exception, not the rule. Choices (a) and (c) overstate restrictions on transmissibility, and choice (d) invents an 'expiration' rule with no legal basis; the general rule under Art. 1178 is that rights acquired from an obligation ARE transmissible, subject only to specific exceptions.

prompt: In which of the following obligations will delay not exist?

choices.text: Positive obligation
Negative obligation
Personal obligation
Real obligation

rationale: Delay (mora) has no application to negative obligations (obligations not to do); a debtor who is obliged not to do something violates the obligation the moment he performs the prohibited act, at which point there is breach, not delay — delay presupposes a positive obligation still capable of being performed late. Positive, personal, and real obligations (choices a, c, d) can all still be subject to delay since they remain capable of late performance; it is only in negative obligations that delay has no application, since violation occurs instantly upon doing the prohibited act.

prompt: Which of the following is considered a civil fruit?

choices.text: Young of animal
Palay
Dividend
Grass

rationale: Civil fruits are those derived from a thing by reason of a juridical relation, such as rents of buildings, the price of leases, and dividends from shares of stock (Art. 442) — as distinguished from natural fruits (spontaneous produce of the earth, young of animals) and industrial fruits (produce of land through cultivation, like palay). Young of animals, palay, and grass (choices a, b, d) are all natural or industrial fruits — the spontaneous or cultivated produce of a thing itself; a dividend, arising from a juridical relation (ownership of shares), is the classic example of a civil fruit.

prompt: They include everything which is produced by a thing, or which is incorporated or attached thereto, either naturally or

choices.text: Alluvium
Accessions
Accessories
Avulsion

rationale: Accessions are everything produced by, or incorporated/attached to, a thing, whether naturally or artificially (Art. 440), encompassing both accessions discreta (fruits) and accessions continua (buildings, plantings, alluvium, etc.) — broader than 'accessories,' which are things joined to a principal for its use, and distinct from alluvium or avulsion, which are specific modes of accession by water action. 'Accessories' (choice c) are separate items merely joined to a principal for its use or ornament, while alluvium and avulsion (choices a, d) are specific, narrower modes of accession caused by water; 'accessions' is the broader term covering everything produced by or attached to a thing, whether naturally or artificially.

prompt: It refers to a right that can be exercised against the whole world thereby allowing an action to recover the ownership or possession of a specific thing regardless of the possessor of such

choices.text: Personal right
Real right
Intangible right
Tangible right

rationale: A real right (jus in re) is enforceable against the whole world (in rem), allowing its holder to follow the thing and recover it regardless of who possesses it, as distinguished from a personal right (jus in personam), which is enforceable only against a specific obligor. A personal right (choice a) may be enforced only against a specific obligor, not the whole world, and 'intangible'/'tangible' (choices c, d) describe the object's nature, not the right itself; a real right is specifically the one enforceable in rem, against whoever possesses the thing.

prompt: D has an outstanding obligation to deliver a specific car to C. If D refuses to deliver the said car to C despite repeated demands, what is the legal remedy available to C?

choices.text: File an action for specific performance plus damages against D
File an action to ask a third person to deliver another car at the expense of D
File an action for annulment of obligation
File an action for reformation of instrument

rationale: Where the object of the obligation is a specific/determinate thing, the creditor may compel the debtor's specific performance of the exact delivery required, in addition to damages for the delay — substitution by another thing at the debtor's expense (a remedy proper to generic obligations) is not available since the thing owed is unique and identified. Because the object is a specific car — not a generic one sourceable from a third person (choice b) — and the obligation is otherwise valid (ruling out annulment or reformation, choices c, d), the proper remedy is to compel D's specific performance of that exact delivery, plus damages.

prompt: D has an obligation to clean the house of C. If D refused to clean the house of C despite repeated demands, what is the legal remedy available to C?

choices.text: File an action for specific performance plus damages
File an action for annulment of obligation
File an action to ask another person to clean the house or allow D to clean the house at the expense of D
File an action for declaration of nullity of obligation

rationale: An obligation to do (render a service), unlike an obligation to give a determinate thing, cannot be the subject of coercive specific performance compelling the debtor's personal act; instead, if the debtor fails to perform, Art. 1167 allows the creditor to have it executed by another at the debtor's expense, plus damages. Because cleaning a house is an obligation to do rather than to give a determinate thing, C cannot obtain direct specific performance compelling D's personal act, nor annul or nullify a valid obligation (choices a, b, d); the proper remedy under Art. 1167 is to have another person do the work at D's expense.

prompt: Which of the following waiver of action is considered valid?

choices.text: Waiver of a civil action for past fraud
Waiver of a civil action for future fraud
Waiver of a civil action for future gross negligence
None of the above

rationale: Under Art. 1171, a waiver of an action to enforce liability arising from fraud is allowed only if the fraud has already been committed (past fraud); a waiver of future fraud, or of future gross negligence (Art. 1171 in relation to Art. 2214/public policy), is void as against public policy, since it would effectively license future bad faith. Waiving liability for FUTURE fraud or future gross negligence (choices b, c) is void as against public policy, since it would excuse anticipated bad faith; only a waiver concerning ALREADY-committed (past) fraud may validly be made, since the injured party's right has already vested.

prompt: It refers to the right of unpaid creditor to exercise all rights and actions of the judgment debtor to recover his claim, except those rights which are inherently personal to the

choices.text: Accion subrogatoria
Accion pauliana
Accion directa
Accion capcatoria

rationale: Accion subrogatoria (Art. 1177) is the right granted to an unpaid creditor, in the absence of other means to satisfy his claim, to exercise all the rights and bring all the actions of his debtor, except those inherently personal to the debtor — distinguished from accion pauliana (rescission of the debtor's fraudulent alienations) and accion directa (a creditor's direct action against a sub-obligor, as in sub-lease or sub-contract situations). Accion pauliana (choice b) rescinds the debtor's fraudulent alienations, and accion directa (choice c) is a creditor's direct action against his debtor's own debtor in specific relations like sub-lease; accion subrogatoria specifically lets an unpaid creditor step into the debtor's shoes to exercise the debtor's own transmissible rights.

prompt: Which of the following obligations is not immediately demandable?

choices.text: Pure obligation
Obligation when debtor's means permit him to do so
Obligation with a resolutory period
Obligation with a resolutory condition

rationale: An obligation whose demandability depends upon a future and uncertain event that lies within the debtor's financial capacity ('when his means permit him to do so') is a conditional obligation with a mixed condition and is not immediately demandable, unlike a pure obligation, which is demandable at once, or obligations with a resolutory period/condition, which are demandable at once and only extinguished upon arrival of the period/condition. Pure obligations and obligations with only a resolutory period or condition (choices a, c, d) are all immediately demandable since nothing suspends their initial enforceability; only an obligation conditioned on 'when the debtor's means permit' requires that condition to first be met.

prompt: Which of the following suspensive conditions will nullify the obligation that is dependent upon them?

choices.text: Condition purely potestative upon the sole will of debtor
Condition purely potestative upon the sole will of creditor
Mixed condition
Casual condition

rationale: Under Art. 1182, a conditional obligation is void when its fulfillment is made to depend upon a suspensive condition that rests purely and exclusively upon the sole will of the debtor (a purely potestative condition); the same rule does not apply where the potestative condition depends on the creditor's will, or where the condition is mixed or merely casual, which remain valid. A condition dependent on the creditor's will, a mixed condition, or a casual condition (choices b, c, d) are all valid; Art. 1182 specifically voids only a suspensive condition depending purely on the sole will of the DEBTOR, since that would make the obligation illusory.

prompt: In conditional reciprocal obligations, what will happen to the fruits and interests during the pendency of the suspensive condition?

choices.text: They shall be forfeited in favor of the state.
They shall inure to the benefit of the debtor.
They shall inure to the benefit of the creditor.
They shall be deemed to have been mutually

rationale: Under Art. 1187 and 1189, during the pendency of a suspensive condition in a reciprocal obligation, the parties are not yet entitled to demand performance, but if the condition is fulfilled, the fruits and interest during the pendency are, as a rule, deemed to have been mutually compensated/offset between the parties (unless the obligation is one to give a determinate thing, in which case Art. 1187 governs fruits received). Forfeiture to the state or exclusive benefit to only one party (choices a, b, c) would unfairly favor one side during the period of uncertainty; because neither party can be said to have earned the fruits/interest while the condition is pending, the law deems them mutually compensated between the parties.

prompt: In an alternative obligation, if the contract does not state who has the right to choose which prestation to perform, who holds that right by default?

choices.text: Both parties must agree on the choice together
The Debtor
The Creditor
The Court

rationale: In an alternative obligation, unless the right to choose has been expressly granted to the creditor (or a third person), the right of choice belongs to the debtor as the default rule (Art. 1200). Requiring mutual agreement or assigning the choice to the creditor or court (choices a, c, d) all contradict the Code's default allocation; Art. 1200 specifically vests the right of choice in the DEBTOR whenever the parties have not stipulated otherwise.

prompt: What happens if the creditor performs an act that makes it impossible for the debtor to choose between the options in an alternative obligation?

choices.text: The debtor may rescind the contract with damages.
The creditor gets to choose for the debtor.
The debtor must still perform the remaining options regardless of the interference.
The obligation is automatically cancelled without any

rationale: Under Art. 1203, if the party who does not have the right of choice (here, the creditor, since the debtor holds it by default) renders it impossible for the debtor to choose by his own acts, the debtor may rescind the contract, with damages, since the creditor's interference frustrated the debtor's statutory right of election. Letting the creditor choose for the debtor, forcing performance of the remaining options despite the interference, or an automatic cancellation without recourse (choices b, c, d) would reward the creditor's own wrongdoing; Art. 1203 instead entitles the debtor to rescind the contract with damages.

prompt: What is the effect if a solidary debtor pays the entire obligation after it has already 'prescribed' (expired due to time)?

choices.text: The other co-debtors must still pay their shares to the one who paid.
The paying debtor loses the right to be reimbursed by the co-debtors.
The creditor must return the money to the debtor.
The co-debtors must pay double because the debt was

rationale: A solidary debtor who, after the debt has already prescribed (and is therefore a mere natural obligation no longer legally demandable), nonetheless pays the entire obligation, is deemed to have made a payment he was not legally compelled to make; consistent with the rule that one who pays a prescribed debt cannot even recover from the original creditor, such a paying debtor likewise loses the right to seek reimbursement from his co-debtors for their shares. Choices (a), (c), and (d) all assume the payment remains fully effective and reimbursable, or even doubles the debt; because the debt could no longer be judicially enforced once prescribed, the paying solidary debtor loses the right to seek reimbursement from his co-debtors.

prompt: What is required for a creditor to demand the penalty stipulated in an obligation with a penal clause?

choices.text: The creditor must prove that the debtor acted with malice or fraud.
The creditor must present receipts proving the exact amount of loss.
The creditor only needs to prove that the debtor breached the obligation.
The creditor must first ask the court to calculate the damages.

rationale: Under Art. 1226, in obligations with a penal clause, proof of actual damages is dispensed with — the creditor need only prove the fact of the debtor's breach of the principal obligation to be entitled to demand the stipulated penalty, unless the penalty itself is subject to reduction for being iniquitous or unconscionable. Requiring proof of malice, exact receipts, or prior judicial computation (choices a, b, d) would defeat the purpose of a penal clause, which dispenses with proof of actual damages; Art. 1226 requires only proof that the debtor breached the principal obligation.

prompt: Which of the following would be considered a third person 'who has an interest' in the fulfillment of the obligation?

choices.text: A random stranger who wants to be generous.
A guarantor.
A neighbor of the creditor.
None of the above

rationale: Under Art. 1302 (in relation to legal subrogation) and the rules on payment by a third person, a person 'with an interest in the fulfillment of the obligation' refers to someone who would suffer a direct legal or financial prejudice if the obligation is not extinguished, such as a guarantor or surety who is himself liable for the debt — unlike a mere stranger or neighbor who has no such stake. A random stranger or mere neighbor (choices a, c) has no legal stake in the obligation's fulfillment; a guarantor, by contrast, would himself become directly liable if the principal debtor defaults, giving him a genuine, legally-recognized interest.

prompt: In a dation in payment, the debtor transfers ownership of a determinate thing to the creditor to satisfy a debt in money. Which of the following statements regarding its governing law is correct?

choices.text: It is governed primarily by the law on donations since the creditor receives property.
It is governed by the law on sales because the debt is considered the purchase price and the property is the object.
It is governed by the law on agency because the creditor acts as an agent to sell the property.
It is governed by the law on partnerships because the parties share in the value of the property.

rationale: Dacion en pago involves the debtor conveying ownership of a determinate thing to satisfy a pre-existing monetary obligation; by express provision (Art. 1245) and settled jurisprudence, it is governed by the law on sales, with the amount of the debt being extinguished treated as the purchase price and the property delivered as the thing sold. Dacion en pago is not governed by donation (no liberality, choice a), agency (the creditor does not act on the debtor's behalf, choice c), or partnership (no sharing of profits, choice d); because the property satisfies a pre-existing money debt, the law on sales governs by analogy.

prompt: Dation in payment and a Contract of Sale share many characteristics. However, they differ in one of the following aspects. Which is it?

choices.text: In a sale, an obligation is created; in dation, an existing obligation is extinguished.
In a sale, there is a transfer of ownership; in dation, there is no transfer of ownership.
In a sale, the cause is a price certain in money; in dation, the cause is the liberality (generosity) of the debtor.
A sale is a real contract, while dation is a consensual contract.

rationale: The fundamental distinction between dacion en pago and an ordinary sale is that in a sale, an obligation is created (the buyer's obligation to pay the price), whereas in dacion en pago, an already-existing obligation is what is being extinguished by the delivery of the property in lieu of money — both remain governed by the law on sales in other respects (e.g., requirement of consent, cause, and object, and both being consensual and involving transfer of ownership). Both dacion en pago and sale involve a transfer of ownership and are governed by the law on sales, so choices (b), (c), and (d) misstate distinctions that do not actually exist; the true distinguishing feature is that a sale CREATES an obligation to pay, while dacion en pago EXTINGUISHES a pre-existing one.

prompt: D borrowed ₱10,000 from C at an annual interest rate of 10%. On the due date, the total debt is ₱11,000 (₱10,000 principal + ₱1,000 interest). If D pays C ₱5,000 without any specific agreement on how it should be applied, how will the payment be legally credited?

choices.text: The entire ₱5,000 will be applied to the principal, leaving ₱1,000 interest unpaid.
₱2,500 will be applied to the principal and ₱2,500 to the interest.
The payment will first cover the ₱1,000 interest, and the remaining ₱4,000 will be applied to the principal.
The payment is void because it does not cover the full amount of the principal.

rationale: Under Art. 1253, if the debt produces interest, payment of the principal is not deemed made until the interest due has first been covered; applying this rule, D's ₱5,000 payment is first applied to the ₱1,000 interest, with the remaining ₱4,000 credited to the principal. Applying the ₱5,000 entirely to the principal (choice a), splitting it evenly (choice b), or voiding the payment for being partial (choice d) all contradict Art. 1253's rule that interest-bearing debts must have their interest satisfied first; ₱1,000 goes to the interest and the remaining ₱4,000 reduces the principal.

prompt: If a creditor voluntarily delivers a private document evidencing a debt to the debtor, what is the legal implication?

choices.text: It implies that the debt has been fully paid in cash.
It implies the renunciation of the action the creditor had against the debtor.
It implies that the creditor is appointing the debtor as his new agent.
It has no legal effect unless a public instrument is executed.

rationale: Under Art. 1271, the voluntary delivery by the creditor to the debtor of a private document evidencing the credit implies the renunciation of the creditor's cause of action against the debtor (a presumption of remission of the debt), unless the debtor proves the delivery was made for some other reason. Voluntary delivery of the debt document does not itself prove cash payment, an agency appointment, or require a public instrument to have effect (choices a, c, d); Art. 1271 instead creates a legal presumption that such delivery signifies the creditor's renunciation of his action against the debtor.

prompt: What is the effect of confusion (merger of the characters of creditor and debtor) in a joint obligation?

choices.text: The entire obligation is extinguished for all parties involved.
The obligation is extinguished only as regards the share corresponding to the specific person in whom the two characters concur.
The obligation remains fully demandable from the remaining joint debtors by the remaining joint creditors.
The joint obligation is automatically converted into a solidary

rationale: In a joint (as opposed to solidary) obligation, if the characters of creditor and debtor merge in one and the same joint debtor (confusion), the obligation is extinguished only as to that particular joint debtor's own proportionate share, since joint obligations are treated as though there were as many distinct debts as there are debtors/creditors (Art. 1208, in relation to Art. 1275). Extinguishing the entire obligation for everyone, keeping it fully demandable from the others, or auto-converting it to solidary (choices a, c, d) all overstate or understate the effect; because a joint obligation is treated as though there were as many separate debts as debtors/creditors, confusion in one joint debtor extinguishes only that debtor's own share.

prompt: When can debts that are rescissible or voidable be compensated against each other?

choices.text: Before they are judicially rescinded or avoided.
Only if both parties explicitly waive their right to sue for rescission.
Never, because these debts are considered defective from the beginning.
Only after a judge has confirmed the validity of both

rationale: Under Art. 1290, debts which are rescissible or voidable may be validly compensated against each other before they have been judicially rescinded or avoided, since until such judicial declaration, these contracts remain valid and produce all their legal effects. Requiring an express waiver of the right to rescind, treating the debts as forever incapable of compensation, or requiring prior judicial confirmation (choices b, c, d) all misstate the rule; because rescissible and voidable contracts remain valid until actually annulled or rescinded, they may be freely compensated before that judicial declaration.

prompt: Under Article 1287, which of the following debts is strictly prohibited from being extinguished by legal compensation?

choices.text: debt arising from a depositum or the obligations of a depositary.
A debt arising from an lease agreement.
A debt arising from a simple loan (mutuum) with interest.
A debt arising from a contract of

rationale: Under Art. 1287, compensation cannot take place against a depositary's or bailee's obligation to return the specific thing deposited, out of respect for the trust nature of a depositum (and similarly, obligations of a bailee in commodatum) — the law does not allow such obligations to be extinguished merely by an offsetting debt. Debts from a lease or an interest-bearing loan (choices b, c) may ordinarily be compensated like any other debt; Art. 1287 singles out depositum and the analogous obligations of a depositary as the debts legal compensation may never extinguish, out of respect for the fiduciary trust involved.

prompt: In a case of 'delegacion,' where the original debtor proposes a new debtor to the creditor, what is the general rule if the new debtor becomes insolvent after the substitution?

choices.text: The creditor can automatically go back to the original debtor to demand payment.
The action of the creditor against the original debtor is NOT revived.
The original debtor must pay half of the debt to show good faith.
The obligation is extinguished for everyone, and the creditor loses the

rationale: Under Art. 1295, if the new debtor substituted in a delegacion becomes insolvent, the creditor's action against the original debtor is revived only if the insolvency was already existing and of public knowledge, or known to the original debtor, at the time he delegated his debt; as a general rule absent these circumstances, the action against the original debtor is NOT revived. Automatic revival of the creditor's action, a mandatory 50% guarantee payment, or total extinguishment for everyone (choices a, c, d) all overstate the original debtor's continuing exposure; once a new debtor is validly substituted, the original debtor is released, and the creditor's action against him is NOT revived even if the new debtor later becomes insolvent, absent bad faith or prior known insolvency.

prompt: As a rule, what happens to the original obligation if the new obligation intended to novate it is void?

choices.text: The parties must create a third obligation to replace both.
The original obligation is extinguished along with the void new one.
The debtor is released from all liability as a penalty to the creditor.
The original obligation subsists and remains

rationale: As a general rule under Art. 1298, if the new obligation intended to substitute (novate) an old one is void, the original obligation subsists and remains in force, since a void novation produces no legal effect and cannot extinguish a valid pre-existing obligation. Requiring a third substitute obligation or excusing the debtor entirely as a penalty on the creditor (choices a, c) invent remedies with no legal basis, and extinguishing the original obligation along with the void new one (choice b) would improperly reward an invalid novation; a void new obligation simply fails to novate, leaving the original obligation intact.

prompt: Legal subrogation is presumed when a creditor pays another creditor who is 'preferred.' Does this subrogation require the debtor's knowledge or consent?

choices.text: Yes, but only if the preferred creditor is a banking institution.
No, but it only applies if the debtor is currently in default (mora).
